## Window of Tolerance {#window-of-tolerance}

The **window of tolerance** is the range where you have enough nervous-system regulation to respond to what is happening and live your day-to-day life. Inside the window, you can usually think, choose, connect, learn, solve problems, and respond rather than simply react. The broader window-of-tolerance model was introduced by Daniel J. Siegel [2].

When you move far enough above or below that workable range, more of your attention and energy can shift toward getting through the moment. At the high end this can become **hyperarousal**. At the low end it can become **hypoarousal**. **Distress tolerance** is especially useful here: the immediate goal is to get through the moment safely, avoid making things worse, and move back toward enough regulation to choose what to do next.

This is a **spectrum**, not a switch between "regulated" and "dysregulated." You do not have to be perfectly calm to be inside your window. You can be stressed, excited, sad, frustrated, or physically activated and still have enough regulation to think and respond effectively.

::: {.callout-note title="About this explanation"}
The descriptions of hyperarousal, hypoarousal, the river analogy, and the shrink-and-expand examples below are paraphrased from the 2020 *Window of Tolerance* infographic by Mind My Peelings [1]. The wording here is original rather than a reproduction of the handout.
:::

![](/assets/distress-tolerance/window-of-tolerance-river.png){.img-fluid fig-alt="A river narrows near hyperarousal, widens through a workable regulated range, and narrows again toward hypoarousal. Calm water, faster currents, rocks, and rapids represent changing conditions across the spectrum." width="1536" height="1024"}

### Think of your window as a river {#window-river}

A useful way to picture the window of tolerance is as a **river in nature**. A healthy river is not perfectly still from beginning to end. It can have calm stretches, faster current, narrow sections, rocks, and rapids. In the same way, being regulated does not mean feeling calm every second. There can be rough or fast-moving parts of the day while you still have enough room to steer, make choices, and stay connected to what matters.

When the river narrows, the same water has less room and the current can become faster and harder to navigate. When your window narrows, stress and emotion can also become harder to manage before you are pushed toward hyperarousal or hypoarousal. When the river widens, there is more room to adjust and recover. Regulation skills can help you navigate a rough stretch, while longer-term habits and skills can gradually make your window more flexible and easier to return to [1].

The goal is therefore not to eliminate every rapid. Life will still contain stress, conflict, grief, excitement, uncertainty, and difficult days. The goal is to build enough regulation that more of the river remains navigable.

### A spectrum from hyperarousal to hypoarousal {#window-states}

- **Hyperarousal:** Your nervous system is highly activated. You may feel anxious, panicky, angry, restless, urgent, overwhelmed, or driven to act immediately. Clear thinking can become harder [1].
- **Higher activation while still in your window:** The water may be moving quickly, but you still have enough regulation to notice what is happening, pause, and choose a response.
- **Calmer, regulated range:** You have enough activation to be alert and engaged without being overwhelmed. Thinking, learning, connecting, and problem-solving are usually easier [1].
- **Lower activation while still in your window:** You may be tired, quiet, slowed down, or needing recovery, while still being able to respond and make choices.
- **Hypoarousal:** Your nervous system is underactivated. You may feel emotionally numb, exhausted, disconnected, frozen, very sleepy, foggy, or have difficulty moving, speaking, or thinking [1].

Distress-tolerance skills can help you move safely away from the extremes of hyperarousal or hypoarousal and back toward a more workable part of the spectrum. A partial shift counts. You do not need to go from overwhelmed to completely calm for a skill to be useful.

If you are not sure what state you are in or what skill might fit, try the [Skill Thermometer](/tool-finder/thermometer/) or browse the [Tool Finder](/tool-finder/).

### What can shrink or widen your window? {#shrink-expand-window}

The original handout highlights **stress and trauma** as experiences that can narrow the window, while **meditation, listening to music, and engaging in hobbies** are examples of activities that may help widen it [1].

Your window is not fixed. Stress, illness, trauma reminders, conflict, exhaustion, pain, hunger, dehydration, isolation, or too much stimulation can make the workable range feel narrower. Recovery, supportive routines, safe connection, and repeated practice with regulation skills can help make it easier to stay within or return to your window.

Many factors can work in either direction depending on **balance, context, and what your nervous system needs that day**.

| Factor | Can support or widen your window | Can shrink or strain your window |
|---|---|---|
| **Sleep** | Enough regular, restorative sleep | Too little, poor-quality, or very irregular sleep |
| **Food** | Regular meals and enough fuel | Hunger, skipping meals, or not eating enough |
| **Water** | Staying adequately hydrated | Dehydration |
| **Exercise and movement** | Manageable, regular movement that fits your body | Too little movement or pushing into pain and exhaustion |
| **Social interaction** | Safe, supportive connection and enough time alone when you need it | Isolation, conflict, unsafe relationships, or too much interaction when already overloaded |
| **Stimulation and recovery** | A workable balance of activity, stimulation, quiet, and rest | Sensory overload, stacked demands, or too little recovery time |
| **Mindfulness and enjoyable activities** | Grounding, meditation, music, hobbies, nature, and other restorative activities | Losing access to activities that help you settle, recover, or reconnect |

More is not always better. Exercise can help and overexertion can drain you. Social connection can help and too much interaction can overwhelm you. Rest can help and long periods of inactivity may leave some people feeling more shut down. The aim is to learn what tends to widen or narrow **your** window and use that information early.

Use the [Window of Tolerance Tool](/tool-finder/window-of-tolerance/) to make a personal list of what narrows your window, what widens it, and which supports are most useful to try first. The tool can be printed or saved as a PDF for quick reference.

Over time, skills from [Wellness](/learn/wellness/), [Interpersonal Effectiveness](/learn/interpersonal-effectiveness/), [Thought Records and CBT](/learn/cbt-anxiety/thought-records.html), and [Emotion Regulation](/learn/emotion-regulation/) can help reduce vulnerabilities, solve recurring problems, and make difficult situations more manageable. [Mindfulness](/learn/mindfulness/) can help across the whole spectrum by making it easier to notice changes in your state earlier and respond more deliberately.

## Objectives {#objectives}

1. Survive crisis situations without making them worse.
2. Accept reality by replacing suffering and being stuck with ordinary pain and the possibility of moving forward.
3. Become free of having to satisfy the demands of your own desires, urges, and intense emotions.

::: {.callout-important title="Sometimes not making things worse is enough"}
During a crisis, success does not have to mean fixing the problem or feeling good. If a skill helps you avoid making the situation worse and gives you time to return to a state where you can choose your next effective step, it is doing its job.
:::
